newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/yen to find foothold after 2-week 10 pct dive.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen to find foothold after 2-week 10 pct dive.

text.p: The dollar is close to finding its footing against the yen after suffering through a shocking 10 percent plunge versus the Japanese currency in little more than two weeks, currency experts said on Thursday.

Still working in the dollar's favor is the beneficial U.S. economic backdrop that helped prop it to a four-and-a-half year high against the yen and a three-year peak versus the mark earlier this month.

Despite recent signs of slower growth, analysts expect continued support from U.S. economic fundamentals and interest rates regardless of the outcome of next week's Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
They are also predicting ongoing support from Japanese capital outflows, which should remain strong as long as Japan continues to run a hefty trade surplus with the United States.

Recent price action makes fresh cycle highs in dollar/yen a long shot for the time being, currency analysts said. But the dollar's downside against the yen may be equally limited in the months ahead once momentum selling dries up.

"I haven't expected this much downside and I don't expect a lot more," said Richard Vullo, vice president on the foreign exchange desk at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank in New York. "I think it's overdone and I don't think it's fundamentally warranted."

As recently as last month, the dollar's two-year upward trajectory against the yen appeared virtually unassailable. Now the markets have begun taking notice of intervention threats from Japanese officials, and banks are revising down their medium-term targets for dollar/yen.
The dollar plunged to a four-and-a-half month low of 114.70 yen in European dealings on Thursday, hurt by massive sales from speculators, Japanese trust banks and exporters.
This week, in its strategy note to clients, Goldman Sachs scrapped its previous dollar/yen target of 130 and said the rate had probably peaked.
"With Fed tightening possibly delayed until late summer, long term interest rate differentials between the U.S. and Japan are likely to narrow further," Goldman Sachs economists said.
However, with Japanese interest rates still at rock-bottom levels, economists said the Japanese investment community will continue to view the U.S. market favorably for quite some time.

Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities, also said downward revisions in the medium-term dollar/yen outlook were warranted. But he cautioned that a major move lower was also unlikely given dollar-supportive fundamentals.
"The strength of the U.S. economy is still neutral to positive for the dollar and the slowdown in the U.S. is not significant enough to change the direction of the exchange rate," Iggo said.

"Japan is also running a trade surplus with the U.S. of roughly $4 billion a month and that's $4 billion that they want to keep in dollars and invest in dollar assets," he added. "It's a constant capital flow."
Analysts also said that recent calls for exchange rate stability indicate Japanese policymakers are loathe to see the yen's appreciation continue unchecked.

Until now, the dollar's drop has failed to reverberate in the domestic or global capital markets. But this could change, analysts said, necessitating stronger dollar-supportive rhetoric from U.S. and foreign officials.
"I think Japanese officials are being deliberately cautious," said John Rothfield, international economist at NationsBanc-CRT in Chicago.

"Certainly the recent price action makes it less likely we'll exceed the recent highs and there should be some adjustment down in forecasts to take account of reality, but not for a significant further strengthening of the yen from here on out."
